name: Domain Stretching
purpose: Adjacent topics — team dynamics, career, product thinking, leadership. Pushes learner boundaries into territory they partially cover.
items: First 1-on-1 as tech lead. Junior dev struggling with imposter syndrome. Shared my experience of feeling lost for 3 months at every new company. Normalizing the struggle helps.
Product manager wants a recommendation engine. Pushed back — not enough user data. Suggested hand-curated rules first, ML after 100k+ interactions. Build simple first.
Conference talk on event-driven architecture. Events should describe what happened, not what should happen next. 'OrderPlaced' not 'SendConfirmationEmail'.
Technical interviews are good at filtering out bad candidates but bad at identifying great ones. Best hire did poorly in algorithms but crushed system design.
Business team wants real-time analytics. Current batch pipeline runs every 6 hours. Evaluating streaming layer vs 15-minute micro-batch. Complexity vs freshness tradeoff.
Writing RFC for microservices migration. The hardest part isn't architecture — it's convincing the team that operational complexity is worth it at our scale.
Onboarding guide: clone repo, run setup, make a small PR, attend standup, pair with each teammate. Goal: productive contribution within 5 days.
Designer frustrated that features look different from mockups. Started a design system with shared tokens. Single source of truth between Figma and code.
Retro feedback: too many meetings, slow PR reviews, unclear priorities. Actions: meeting-free Wednesdays, rotating reviewer schedule, weekly priority stack-rank.
Debating open-sourcing internal tools. Pros: community contributions, hiring signal. Cons: maintenance burden, security review. Starting with one low-risk library.
Customer support escalation: users lose drafts on accidental navigation. Implementing auto-save with localStorage, then debounced server persistence.
Explained technical debt to CEO in business terms. 'Every new payment feature takes 3 weeks instead of 1 because of shortcuts from 2022.' Got refactor approved.
Sprint planning took 3 hours. We underestimate because we don't account for review, QA, and deploy overhead. Adding 1.3x buffer multiplier.
Mobile team wants to share business logic with web. Three options: shared TS library, API-first, or React Native. Each has different tradeoffs.
Performance reviews — struggle to quantify individual impact. Incidents prevented, deploy frequency, MTTR are better metrics but they're team-level.
Mentoring mid-level dev on system design. Biggest gap isn't knowledge — it's understanding tradeoffs. Can describe consistent hashing but not when to use it.
Product wants A/B testing framework. With 2000 DAU, most tests need months for significance. Qualitative feedback might be better at this stage.
SLA is 99.9%, we're at 99.7% from the DNS incident. Writing post-mortem with remediation: separate DNS zones, automated failover, propagation alerts.
Started keeping a decision journal. For each choice: what, why, alternatives considered, what would make me reverse it. Review quarterly.
Previous lead left no documentation. Spent a week reverse-engineering the deploy pipeline. 14 env vars, 3 unused, 2 misspelled but critical.
Teaching the team about Conway's Law. Our microservices mirror our org structure, which isn't intentional. The payment team's service is a monolith because they're one person.
The product owner keeps changing requirements mid-sprint. Had a direct conversation about the cost of context switching. Agreed on a change freeze after sprint day 3.
Ran a blameless post-mortem for the outage. The key question isn't 'who caused it' but 'what made it possible for this to happen.' Found 3 systemic gaps.
Promoted a senior engineer to staff. The hardest part of the conversation: explaining that staff isn't about writing more code, it's about multiplying the team's output.
Our estimation accuracy is terrible. Started tracking estimate vs actual for every ticket. After 20 data points, found we consistently underestimate by 2.3x. Now we multiply.
Had to say no to a feature the CEO wanted. Built a one-pager showing the opportunity cost: building Feature X means not shipping Features Y and Z which drive more revenue.
The QA team is overwhelmed. They manually test every PR. Starting to automate the regression suite — 80% of manual tests can be automated with Playwright.
Tech debt scoring system: each tech debt item gets scored on blast radius (how many features it affects), developer pain (how often devs complain), and fix effort. Prioritize by score/effort.
Introduced mob programming for complex features. 3-4 devs, one screen, rotating driver every 15 minutes. Slower per-person but the code quality is notably higher and needs fewer review cycles.
Our standups are 25 minutes for 8 people. Nobody listens to anyone else's update. Switched to async standups in Slack with a bot. Freed up 2 hours per week per person.
Customer churn analysis shows most users leave during the first week. The activation gap: they sign up, get confused by the empty state, and never come back. Need a guided first experience.
Building the business case for a platform rewrite. The current system works but every feature takes 3x longer than it should. Need to show the compounding cost of not rewriting.
Feedback from skip-level meeting: engineers feel disconnected from users. Starting a 'customer shadow' program where each engineer sits with support for half a day per month.
Our incident response is ad hoc. Defining severity levels (SEV1-4), response time expectations, communication templates, and escalation paths. Boring but essential.
The gap between design and engineering is growing. Designers create pixel-perfect mockups that ignore API constraints. Engineers build features that ignore design intent. Need a shared language.
Introduced RFC process for changes that affect multiple teams. Template: problem, proposed solution, alternatives considered, rollout plan. Forces clear thinking before coding.
Our on-call rotation is burning people out. 1 week on, 3 weeks off, but the on-call week averages 3 pages per night. Need to fix the noisy alerts before adding more people to the rotation.
Struggling with hiring for a senior backend role. 50 applicants, 10 phone screens, 4 on-sites, 0 offers. Either our bar is too high or our job description is attracting the wrong candidates.
Ran a team health check survey. Lowest scores: psychological safety (6/10) and sustainable pace (5/10). These are more important than any technical metric.
The most productive team change we made: cutting meeting time by 40% and adding 2-hour focus blocks every morning. Output didn't just stay the same — it increased measurably.

Conducted a value stream mapping exercise for our deployment process. Found that 60% of lead time is waiting — waiting for review, waiting for QA, waiting for deploy window. The actual work takes 2 hours.
Our architecture review board has become a bottleneck. 3-week wait for approval. Switched to lightweight 'architecture advice' — teams consult an architect but make their own decisions.
Running a book club on 'Team Topologies'. The stream-aligned team concept resonates — teams should be organized around business capabilities, not technical layers.
Started writing monthly engineering newsletters for the company. Non-technical stakeholders now understand what we're building and why. Reduced 'why is this taking so long?' questions by half.
Career framework rollout. Defined expectations for each level (junior → mid → senior → staff → principal). Clear promotion criteria reduces ambiguity and perceived unfairness.
Our staging environment is perpetually broken. Nobody owns it, everybody deploys to it. Introduced per-PR preview environments. Staging is now reserved for final integration testing.
Trying to build a culture of writing. Design docs, decision records, post-mortems, runbooks. The resistance is real — 'I'd rather just code.' But institutional memory requires written records.
Lunch-and-learn session on database internals. Explained B-trees, write-ahead logs, and MVCC. Three engineers came up afterward saying it changed how they think about query optimization.
The biggest productivity gain this quarter wasn't a tool or process — it was clarifying team boundaries. When people know exactly what they own, they stop waiting for permission.
Introduced 'tech debt Fridays' — 20% time every Friday for paying down technical debt. After 2 months, build times halved and the flaky test count dropped from 15 to 2.

Running a retrospective on our retrospectives. The format is stale — same 3 people talk, same issues raised, rarely leads to change. Trying a new format: silent brainstorm, dot vote, commit to one action.
Our junior developers are afraid to ask questions in public channels. Created a #no-stupid-questions channel with an explicit norm: every question is welcome, no judgment. Activity exploded.
Evaluating whether to build or buy our notification system. Build: full control, 3 months. Buy: faster, $500/month, less flexible. Chose buy — our competitive advantage isn't sending emails.
Had a difficult conversation with a high-performer who's toxic in code reviews. The quality of their feedback is excellent but the delivery is demoralizing. Agreed on a 'feedback sandwich' approach.
Organized a hackathon focused on developer experience. Top 3 projects: one-command local setup, visual API explorer, and automated PR description generator. All shipped within a month.
Our definition of done was vague. Now explicit: code reviewed, tests passing, documentation updated, feature flagged, monitoring dashboard added, runbook entry written.
The hardest part of being a tech lead isn't the technical decisions — it's managing up. Translating engineering constraints into business language that executives can act on.
Started pair architecture sessions. Before any feature work, two engineers spend 30 minutes whiteboarding the approach. Catches design mistakes early. Costs 1 hour, saves 10.
Our team morale took a hit after the reorg. Two strong engineers left. Responding by being transparent about the roadmap and giving remaining engineers more autonomy over technical choices.
Created an 'engineering principles' doc as a team. Five principles we all agreed on. Now when we disagree on an approach, we reference the principles instead of arguing from preference.
Feedback from user research: our API documentation is 'technically accurate but practically useless.' Users want recipes and examples, not just reference docs. Overhauling the getting-started guide.
Measured our deployment frequency: 2.3 deploys per week. DORA metrics say elite teams deploy multiple times per day. The gap isn't technical — it's confidence. We don't trust our test suite enough.

Helped a mid-level engineer write their first technical blog post. The draft was overly cautious — 'in my limited experience.' Coached them to state their conclusions confidently. The post got 50k reads.
Team ritual: every Friday we share one thing we learned that week. Quick round, 2 minutes each. Creates a culture of continuous learning and makes it safe to admit you didn't know something.
Our documentation lives in 4 places: Confluence, Notion, README files, and Google Docs. Nobody knows where to find anything. Consolidating everything to a single docs-as-code repo.

The engineering manager asked me to justify our testing strategy to the VP. Prepared data: each bug caught in CI costs $100 to fix. Each bug caught in production costs $10,000. Tests pay for themselves 100x.
Ran a dependency mapping workshop. Drew all inter-service dependencies on a whiteboard. Found a circular dependency between 3 services that nobody realized existed. Untangling it now.
Our sprint velocity fluctuates wildly: 30 points, 45 points, 20 points, 50 points. The inconsistency makes planning impossible. Root cause: unplanned work isn't being tracked or sized.
Created a 'tech radar' for our organization. Categorized technologies into Adopt, Trial, Assess, Hold. Gives teams guidance without being prescriptive. Updated quarterly.
The most undervalued engineering skill: writing clear commit messages. A good message explains why, not what. 'Fix null check' vs 'Prevent crash when user deletes account during checkout flow.'
Our engineering org doubled in size this year. What worked for 10 engineers doesn't work for 20. Adding more structure: team charters, documented processes, explicit ownership maps.
